analysis.one_liner: Bans neonicotinoid insecticides on national wildlife refuges.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the pesticide ban 17–13, but the bill sat on the House calendar and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Neonicotinoids are a class of insecticides chemically similar to nicotine, widely used in agriculture and linked in scientific studies to declines in bees and other pollinators. In 2014 the Fish and Wildlife Service banned them on national wildlife refuges, but the Trump administration reversed that policy in 2018, allowing their use again. This bill would write a permanent ban into the law governing the refuge system, so no administration could quietly restore the pesticides.
analysis.who_benefits: People who visit or live near the 150-plus million acres of the National Wildlife Refuge System, pollinators and the wildlife that depends on them, and beekeepers whose hives are harmed when these insecticides drift into forage.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a section to the National Wildlife Refuge System Administration Act of 1966 stating that no person may use a neonicotinoid anywhere in the System, making the ban permanent law rather than agency policy that can be reversed.

Neonicotinoids are neuroactive insecticides; studies have linked them to harm to bees and other pollinators, which underpin both wild ecosystems and about a third of the food supply through crop pollination.
The bill passed out of committee with a bipartisan vote of 17–13, showing support beyond the sponsor's party.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers that sell neonicotinoids, and some farming operations that grow crops on refuge lands under cooperative agreements and use these insecticides for pest control.
analysis.who_pays_short: Neonicotinoid makers and refuge-land farm operators

drawbacks.text: Some farm cooperatives that lease refuge land to grow crops would lose one class of pest-control tools, and could face crop losses or have to switch to costlier or more labor-intensive alternatives.

The Fish and Wildlife Service's current policy already requires integrated pest management reviews of pesticide use on refuges, so supporters of the status quo argue case-by-case review is sufficient and a flat statutory ban removes agency flexibility.

Industry groups have long argued that the evidence linking neonicotinoids to pollinator decline at field-realistic doses is contested, which is a cost an honest supporter must weigh against the precautionary case for the ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is protecting pollinators and wildlife across more than 150 million acres of public land and making a former agency policy durable. The cost is real but narrow: a limited number of refuge farming operations lose one pesticide option. This is a modest, targeted environmental protection, not a sweeping regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The Natural Resources Committee approved it in November 2019, but the report didn't come out until August 2020, and House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2019 and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
After a subcommittee hearing and being discharged from subcommittee, the committee ordered the bill reported on November 20, 2019 by a vote of 17–13.
The committee formally reported the bill on August 7, 2020, with House Report 116-468, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting floor action.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote on the House floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 45 cosponsors, 44 Democrats and 1 Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neonicotinoid manufacturers and growers who use the insecticides on refuge land are better off, because the status quo permitting their use remained in place. People who wanted pollinators protected on public lands gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and the status quo

against.what_they_did: The industry benefits from the bill's failure; its alignment against the ban is well documented in the broader pesticide policy debate, though no industry lobbying on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 17–13 with the Democratic majority in favor; only 1 of the bill's 45 cosponsors was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill removes refuges — tens of millions of acres of public farmland and habitat — as a place these companies can sell their products. Pollinator protection is exactly what the chemicals' scientific critics cite against them, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.
Commercial hives pollinate crops nationwide, and neonicotinoid exposure on or near refuge land is a documented risk to them. Their gain is the public's gain.

Cooperative farming programs on refuges would lose a cheap, effective insecticide and could face higher pest-control costs, but banning the chemical on surrounding land can also reduce exposure of the hives those farms depend on for pollination.
